zh.title: 犯过大错后，还能重新开始吗？有人用十年回家，有人用一生，才终于回到自己｜奥德赛
zh.excerpt: 错误有代价，选择有后果；真正能回应过去的，是今天之后你选择成为怎样的人。
zh.content:
THE LONG WAY HOME

错误有代价，选择有后果。但真正能回应过去的，是今天之后，你选择成为怎样的人。

![有人用十年回家，有人用一生，才终于回到自己](/assets/notes/2026-08-26-odyssey-long-way-home/image-01.png)

看完《奥德赛》，我很久没有说话。

脑子里一直反复出现一句话：

> 人非圣贤，孰能无过。人都会犯错，英雄与神也不例外。

只是后来才慢慢明白，真正残酷的从来不是“犯错”本身。

而是——

> 错误有代价，选择有后果。

有些代价几个月就能过去，有些要花很多年。

还有一些错误，你可能用尽一生，也无法让它彻底消失。

## CHAPTER 01｜我们总以为，《奥德赛》讲的是回家

奥德修斯离开故乡伊萨卡，参加了十年的特洛伊战争。

战争结束以后，他又在海上漂泊了十年。

遇见风暴、怪物、诱惑、死亡，也一次又一次为自己的骄傲、欲望和选择付出代价。

二十年后，他终于回到了家。

年轻时看这样的故事，我们很容易把它理解成一个英雄历尽艰险、最终凯旋的冒险故事。

但现在再看，我突然觉得：

> 《奥德赛》真正讲的，也许从来不是一个人如何战胜世界。

而是一个人在经历了欲望、骄傲、错误、失去之后，

> 还能不能找到回去的路。

而所谓“回去”，也不只是回到伊萨卡。

更重要的是：

> 回到自己。

![错误有代价，但我们仍可以选择接下来驶向哪里](/assets/notes/2026-08-26-odyssey-long-way-home/image-02.png)

## CHAPTER 02｜犯错以后，你愿不愿意承担代价

人总希望自己的过去是完整的。

希望每一次选择都是正确的，每一步都没有走错，每一个重要的人都没有辜负。

可真实的人生不是这样。

我们都会在某个时刻做出错误的判断。

会因为年轻、无知、自负、欲望、恐惧，甚至只是某一瞬间的软弱，做出后来无法改变的事。

有些错误很小。

有些错误，真的会改变人生。

以前我总觉得，一个人犯了错以后，只要知道错了，就应该学会“放下”。

后来才发现，没有这么简单。

真正的反省，并不是不断告诉自己：

“过去就过去了。”

“当时我也没办法。”

“别再想了。”

如果一件事真的造成了后果，这些话甚至可能让人更难受。

因为真正的和解，从来不是否认。

而是：

> 我承认，那是我做的。

> 我承认，它有后果。

> 我承认，有些东西再也回不来了。

然后问自己一个更难的问题：

> 接下来，我准备怎样活？

![承担不是永远惩罚自己，而是认真修补还能修补的部分](/assets/notes/2026-08-26-odyssey-long-way-home/image-03.png)

## CHAPTER 03｜痛苦，不等于承担

这些年我慢慢意识到一件事。

人犯过一个很大的错误以后，很容易把“承担责任”和“惩罚自己”混在一起。

我们会觉得：

如果我不再痛苦，是不是说明我已经忘记了？

如果我重新快乐，是不是对不起过去？

如果我过得越来越好，是不是意味着我没有真正悔过？

于是我们在心里建了一座法庭。

自己既是被告，也是法官。

一遍又一遍审判自己。

甚至会产生一种隐秘的信念：

> 只要我一直痛苦，就好像还在偿还。

但后来我才明白：

> 痛苦本身，并不能偿还过去。

你再难过十年，也无法让已经发生的事情没有发生。

你再责罚自己一万次，也无法让时间倒流。

真正能够回应过去的，只有今天之后，你选择成为怎样的人。

该承担的责任，去承担。

还能弥补的，尽量弥补。

该道歉的，道歉。

该改变的，改变。

然后把那些无法再改变的部分，留在时间里。

这不是逃避。

恰恰可能是最艰难的一种承担。

![归来不是回到从前，而是带着变化重新进入生活](/assets/notes/2026-08-26-odyssey-long-way-home/image-04.png)

## CHAPTER 04｜回家，不是回到一切发生以前

《奥德赛》最打动我的地方，是奥德修斯最后真的回到了伊萨卡。

但那已经不是二十年前的伊萨卡了。

他的儿子已经长大。

妻子等了二十年。

朋友、家庭、秩序，全都发生了变化。

而他自己，更不可能还是二十年前那个出发的人。

所以所谓“归来”，从来不是：

> 终于回到了那个什么都还没有发生的自己。

因为那个人已经不存在了。

我们总幻想有一天能够彻底治愈过去，然后重新变成犯错之前的那个自己。

可人生没有这样的按钮。

真正的归来，是：

> 带着发生过的一切，继续回来生活。

带着伤。

带着遗憾。

带着代价。

带着那些无法撤回的选择。

同时，也带着这些年一点一点长出来的新东西。

理解。

克制。

谦卑。

责任。

慈悲。

以及终于开始能够接受自己的勇气。

## CHAPTER 05｜与自己和解，不是判自己无罪

我以前对“和解”这个词有一种误解。

好像与自己和解，就是最终说服自己：

“其实那件事没那么严重，圣贤和神都会犯错。”

现在我越来越觉得，不是。

真正的自我和解，并不是判自己无罪。

而是终于能够同时容纳两个事实：

> 我确实做错过。

和：

> 我依然可以继续成为一个更好的人。

这两句话之间，有时候隔着十年。

有时候隔着半生。

甚至有人花了一辈子，也没有真正走完。

所以《奥德赛》里最让我触动的，不再是那些怪物、海洋和战争。

而是一个人漂泊那么久以后，

> 还愿意回家。

![世界还没有完全变好，生命已经重新开始向前](/assets/notes/2026-08-26-odyssey-long-way-home/image-05.png)

## CHAPTER 06｜有人用十年回家，有人用一生

今天想到上午聊《易经》时的一个字：

> 复。

复，不是恢复原状。

不是把人生重新倒带。

《易经》里的“复”，只是黑暗走到很深以后，最下面重新出现了一根小小的阳爻。

世界还没有变好。

春天还没有真正到来。

只是生命重新开始向前。

我越来越喜欢这个意象。

因为很多时候，我们真正需要的可能不是立刻“否极泰来”。

而只是：

> 先回来一点。

今天比昨天多接受自己一点。

今天比昨天少责罚自己一点。

今天愿意重新做一件正确的事。

今天愿意重新爱一个人。

今天愿意重新相信生活。

也许所谓人生的重建，本来就是这样。

不是突然翻篇。

而是一寸一寸地回来。

人非圣贤，孰能无过。

人都会犯错，英雄与神也不例外。

> 错误有代价，选择有后果，而成长，就是学会承担。

犯错以后，你愿不愿意承认代价；

失去以后，你还愿不愿意继续走；

走了很远以后，你还能不能认出自己。

我想，这可能就是《奥德赛》最后留给我的东西。

> 接受那个已经经历过欲望、骄傲、错误和失去的自己。

不是忘记。

不是开脱。

也不是假装一切从未发生。

而是在某一天，终于可以对过去的自己说：

> 我不会否认你。

> 但我也不会再让你决定我的余生。

有人用十年回家。

有人用一生。

而人生真正漫长的那场奥德赛，

也许就是——

> 穿过所有已经无法改变的过去，最终重新找到自己是谁。

认识自己。

接纳自己。

成为自己。

活出自己。

## EPILOGUE｜在 WonderElian，继续这条回到自己的路

这也是我做“一休、不二、三慢”的原因。

一休，先照顾身体，安顿情绪，再继续前行。

不二，不评判，没有对错好坏，接纳高峰与低谷，拥抱完整，而不是追求完美。

三慢，慢下来，慢慢来，慢慢成为。

如果你也正在学习认识自己、接纳自己、成为自己，并把真实的自己活出来，欢迎来到 WonderElian。

en.label: FIELD NOTE · 05
en.title: After a Serious Mistake, Can You Begin Again? Some Take Ten Years to Return Home; Others a Lifetime to Return to Themselves | The Odyssey
en.excerpt: Mistakes carry a price, and choices have consequences. What truly answers the past is the person you choose to become from this day forward.
en.content:
THE LONG WAY HOME

Mistakes carry a price, and choices have consequences. Yet what truly answers the past is the person you choose to become from this day forward.

![Some take ten years to return home; others a lifetime to return to themselves](/assets/notes/2026-08-26-odyssey-long-way-home/image-01.png)

After watching The Odyssey, I sat in silence for a long time.

One thought kept returning:

> No one is beyond error. We all make mistakes; heroes and gods are no exception.

Only later did I begin to understand that the cruelest thing is rarely the mistake itself.

It is this:

> Mistakes carry a price, and choices have consequences.

Some prices pass in a matter of months. Others take years.

And there are mistakes that even a lifetime may not make disappear completely.

## CHAPTER 01｜We Think The Odyssey Is a Story About Coming Home

Odysseus leaves Ithaca to fight in the Trojan War, which lasts ten years.

When the war ends, he spends another ten years wandering at sea.

He meets storms, monsters, temptation, and death. Again and again, he pays for his pride, his desire, and his choices.

After twenty years, he finally reaches home.

When we are young, it is easy to read this as an adventure about a hero who survives every trial and returns in triumph.

But watching it now, I found myself thinking:

> Perhaps The Odyssey was never really about one man defeating the world.

Perhaps it is about whether, after desire, pride, error, and loss,

> a person can still find the way back.

And “back” does not mean Ithaca alone.

More than anything, it means:

> back to yourself.

![Mistakes carry a price, but we can still choose where we sail next](/assets/notes/2026-08-26-odyssey-long-way-home/image-02.png)

## CHAPTER 02｜After a Mistake, Are You Willing to Bear Its Cost?

We want the story of our past to feel whole.

We want every choice to have been right, every step free of error, every person who mattered left unhurt by us.

Real life is not like that.

At some point, all of us make the wrong judgment.

Youth, ignorance, pride, desire, fear—or simply one moment of weakness—can lead us to do something that cannot later be undone.

Some mistakes are small.

Some really do change a life.

I used to think that once someone understood a mistake, the next lesson was simply to “let it go.”

Later I learned that it is not so simple.

Real reflection is not the endless repetition of reassuring phrases:

“What is past is past.”

“I had no other choice then.”

“Stop thinking about it.”

When something has caused real consequences, those words may make the pain worse.

Reconciliation does not begin with denial.

It begins here:

> I acknowledge that I did it.

> I acknowledge that it had consequences.

> I acknowledge that some things will never return.

Then comes the harder question:

> How am I prepared to live now?

![Responsibility is not endless self-punishment; it is repairing, with care, what can still be repaired](/assets/notes/2026-08-26-odyssey-long-way-home/image-03.png)

## CHAPTER 03｜Pain Is Not the Same as Responsibility

Over the years, I have slowly come to see something.

After a serious mistake, it is easy to confuse taking responsibility with punishing yourself.

We wonder:

If I stop suffering, does that mean I have forgotten?

If I allow myself to be happy again, am I betraying the past?

If my life becomes better, does that mean my remorse was never real?

So we build a courtroom inside ourselves.

We become both defendant and judge.

We put ourselves on trial again and again.

Sometimes a private conviction takes root:

> If I keep suffering, perhaps I am still paying what I owe.

But eventually I understood:

> Pain itself cannot repay the past.

Ten more years of sorrow will not make the event unhappen.

Punishing yourself ten thousand times will not turn time back.

The only honest answer to the past is the person you choose to become from this day forward.

Take the responsibility that is yours.

Repair what can still be repaired.

Offer the apology that is owed.

Make the change that is needed.

Then leave what can no longer be changed with time.

This is not escape.

It may be the most difficult form of responsibility there is.

![Returning is not going back to who you were, but re-entering life as the person you have become](/assets/notes/2026-08-26-odyssey-long-way-home/image-04.png)

## CHAPTER 04｜Coming Home Does Not Mean Returning to Before

What moves me most in The Odyssey is that Odysseus really does return to Ithaca.

But it is no longer the Ithaca he left twenty years before.

His son has grown.

His wife has waited for twenty years.

Friendships, family, and the order of things have all changed.

And he cannot possibly be the man who first set out.

So returning never means:

> At last, I have become the person I was before any of it happened.

That person no longer exists.

We often imagine that one day we will heal the past completely and become who we were before the mistake.

Life has no such button.

To return, in the truest sense, is this:

> To carry everything that happened and come back to life anyway.

With the wound.

With regret.

With the price that was paid.

With choices that cannot be withdrawn.

And also with what has quietly grown over the years:

Understanding.

Restraint.

Humility.

Responsibility.

Compassion.

And, at last, the courage to begin accepting yourself.

## CHAPTER 05｜Making Peace with Yourself Is Not a Verdict of Innocence

I once misunderstood the phrase “making peace with yourself.”

I thought it meant finally persuading yourself:

“It was not really that serious. Even sages and gods make mistakes.”

I no longer believe that.

Real reconciliation with yourself is not a verdict of innocence.

It is the ability to hold two truths at once:

> I really did something wrong.

And:

> I can still go on becoming a better person.

Sometimes those two sentences are ten years apart.

Sometimes half a lifetime lies between them.

Some people spend their whole lives without completing the distance.

That is why the monsters, oceans, and wars are no longer what move me most in The Odyssey.

What moves me is that, after wandering for so long,

> someone is still willing to go home.

![The world is not yet entirely better, but life has begun moving forward again](/assets/notes/2026-08-26-odyssey-long-way-home/image-05.png)

## CHAPTER 06｜Some Take Ten Years to Return Home; Others a Lifetime

This morning, while talking about the I Ching, I found myself thinking about one character:

> 复 — return.

Return does not mean restoring everything to its original state.

It does not mean rewinding a life.

In the I Ching, “return” is the first small unbroken line reappearing at the very bottom after darkness has reached its depth.

The world has not become better yet.

Spring has not truly arrived.

Life has simply begun moving forward again.

I have grown increasingly fond of this image.

Because often what we need is not an immediate reversal from the worst fortune to the best.

It is simply this:

> Come back a little first.

Accept yourself a little more today than yesterday.

Punish yourself a little less today than yesterday.

Choose one right thing again today.

Be willing to love someone again today.

Be willing to believe in life again today.

Perhaps rebuilding a life has always happened this way.

Not by turning the page all at once.

But by returning, inch by inch.

No one is beyond error.

We all make mistakes; heroes and gods are no exception.

> Mistakes carry a price, choices have consequences, and growth means learning to bear them.

After the mistake, are you willing to acknowledge the cost?

After the loss, are you still willing to walk on?

After travelling so far, can you still recognize yourself?

I think this may be what The Odyssey finally left with me.

> Accept the self who has already passed through desire, pride, error, and loss.

Not forgetting.

Not excusing.

Not pretending that nothing happened.

But reaching a day when you can finally say to your former self:

> I will not deny you.

> But I will not let you decide the rest of my life.

Some take ten years to return home.

Some take a lifetime.

And perhaps the longest odyssey of a human life is this:

> To cross everything in the past that can no longer be changed, and finally find again who you are.

Know yourself.

Accept yourself.

Become yourself.

Live as yourself.

## EPILOGUE｜At WonderElian, Continuing the Way Back to Yourself

This is also why I made Yixiu, Bu'er, and Sanman.

Yixiu means pausing first: care for the body, settle the emotions, then continue.

Bu'er means not judging everything as right or wrong, good or bad: accept the peaks and the valleys, and embrace wholeness instead of chasing perfection.

Sanman means slowing down: take your time, and slowly become.

If you, too, are learning to know yourself, accept yourself, become yourself, and live as your real self, welcome to WonderElian.
